name: alist-copy
summary: A fresh association list whose spine AND whose entry pairs are all new, so nothing in it is shared with the original.
explanation: Ordinary list-copy duplicates the spine and leaves the elements alone. For an association list that is not enough, because the elements ARE pairs and a set-cdr! on one of them would reach through the copy into the original. alist-copy goes one level deeper: it makes a new spine and a new (key . datum) pair for every entry. The keys and the data themselves are still shared -- it is two levels deep, not infinitely deep -- so copying an alist whose values are vectors still leaves those vectors aliased. The verb exists for exactly one reason: to make an alist you can mutate in place without a caller elsewhere seeing the change. If you never mutate entries, you never need it, because every functional update already produces a new list. That is the honest test for whether to reach for it: if the next thing you write is set-cdr!, copy first; if the next thing you write is alist-cons, do not, because the sharing is the whole point of alist-cons.

examples.note: ((a . 1) (b . 2)) -- it looks identical, and that is the point: the difference is identity, not contents.

examples.code:
(define original (list (cons 'a 1) (cons 'b 2)))
(define duplicate (alist-copy original))
(display (list 'equal (equal? duplicate original)
               'same-list (eq? duplicate original)
               'same-entry (eq? (car duplicate) (car original))))
(newline)
examples.note: (equal #t same-list #f same-entry #f) -- equal? everywhere, eq? nowhere. Both levels were rebuilt.

examples.code:
(define shared-vector (vector 9 9))
(define original (list (cons 'v shared-vector)))
(define duplicate (alist-copy original))
(vector-set! (cdr (car duplicate)) 0 1)
(display (list 'copy (vector->list (cdr (car duplicate)))
               'original (vector->list (cdr (car original)))))
(newline)
examples.note: (copy (1 9) original (1 9)) -- the copy is two levels deep, so the VALUE is still shared. Writing through it is visible from both.

caveats: It is two levels deep, not deep. Keys and data are shared. If a datum is a vector, a string or another list, mutating it is visible from both alists.
It is O(n) in both time and allocation, and it allocates 2n pairs, not n. Copying an alist inside a loop is a common accidental quadratic.
It does not deduplicate. An alist with two pairs for the same key copies to an alist with two pairs for the same key.
It does not sort or reorder. The copy has the same order, which matters because assq depends on order.
Copying is unnecessary for purely functional use. alist-cons, alist-delete and the fold-based rebuilds all already produce fresh structure; the copy is only for the mutation case.
usecases: Handing an alist to code that may set-cdr! its entries, without letting that reach your copy.
Snapshotting a mutable configuration before a speculative change, so it can be restored by rebinding.
Making a working copy for a destructive algorithm so that the destructive version stays usable.

learn.concept: Copy depth is a decision, not a detail: one level protects the spine, two levels protect the entries, and nothing protects the values unless you say so.
learn.progression: Compare a copy to its original with equal? and see #t, then with eq? and see #f -- that is the whole idea. Then put a vector in a datum, mutate it through the copy, and watch the original change. Now you know what 'shallow' actually costs, and you know which level you are protecting.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (snapshot settings) (alist-copy settings))
(define live (list (cons 'volume 5) (cons 'theme 'light)))
(define saved (snapshot live))
(set-cdr! (assq 'volume live) 11)
(display (list 'live (cdr (assq 'volume live))
               'saved (cdr (assq 'volume saved))
               'theme-still (cdr (assq 'theme saved))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (independent? f)
  (let ((g (alist-copy f)))
    (list 'same-graph (equal? g f)
          'same-object (eq? g f)
          'points (length g))))
(display (list (independent? '((1 . 1) (2 . 4) (3 . 9))) (independent? '())))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define original (list (cons 'a (list 1 2))))
(define shallow (list-copy original))
(define deeper (alist-copy original))
(display (list 'spine-shared (eq? (car shallow) (car original))
               'entry-rebuilt (not (eq? (car deeper) (car original)))
               'datum-still-shared (eq? (cdr (car deeper)) (cdr (car original)))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A settings object is about to be mutated in place and the previous state has to survive. Candidates: alist-copy (rebuilds spine and entries, so a set-cdr! on any entry cannot reach the snapshot -- exactly the level of protection needed here), list-copy (rebuilds the spine only, and the entries stay shared, so set-cdr! on an entry writes through both and the snapshot is a lie), rebuilding with map and cons (identical result, more code, and easy to get one level wrong), keeping a hash table and copying that instead (fine, but then assq order and shadowing are gone), not copying at all and using alist-cons for the change (best answer when mutation is optional -- but here it is not). alist-copy is the pick precisely because mutation is the requirement.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: a snapshot taken before a set-cdr!, showing the live value moved and the saved one did not. math: the copy read as a duplicate of a finite map -- same graph, different object -- including the empty map, where copying is still meaningful and still cheap. cs: the three-way comparison that shows exactly how deep the copy goes; list-copy shares the entry, alist-copy rebuilds it, and NEITHER rebuilds the datum.
row-2-audit.meta: Why alist-copy and not list-copy: this is the one place where the difference is not academic. The bug it prevents -- a snapshot that silently tracks the original because only the spine was copied -- is invisible until something mutates, which is usually in production.
row-2-audit.eng: A snapshot that shares its entries is not a snapshot. The cost of finding that out later is much higher than the 2n pairs.
row-2-audit.math: Two representations of the same finite map are equal? but not eq?. Identity and value are different questions and a language that conflates them cannot express aliasing at all.
row-2-audit.cs: Copy depth is the whole subject. list-copy, alist-copy and a true deep copy are three different contracts, and picking the wrong one produces a bug that only appears under mutation.

row-3-dimension.setup: Making something that reads the same as the original but cannot be reached from it, and deciding how far down 'cannot be reached' goes.

rungs.code:
(define src '((a . 1) (b . 2)))
(define dst (alist-copy src))
(display (list dst (equal? dst src) (eq? dst src)))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a bench of calibration offsets in millimetres that a technician is about to adjust
rungs.code:
(define bench (list (cons 'gauge-1 0.2) (cons 'gauge-2 -0.1)))
(define as-found (alist-copy bench))
(set-cdr! (assq 'gauge-1 bench) 0.0)
(display (list 'as-left (cdr (assq 'gauge-1 bench))
               'as-found (cdr (assq 'gauge-1 as-found))
               'drift (- (cdr (assq 'gauge-1 as-found)) (cdr (assq 'gauge-1 bench)))))
(newline)

rungs.domain: transactional state: a speculative edit that has to be committable or discardable
rungs.code:
(define (begin-txn state) (alist-copy state))
(define committed (list (cons 'balance 100) (cons 'holds 0)))
(define working (begin-txn committed))
(set-cdr! (assq 'balance working) 40)
(set-cdr! (assq 'holds working) 60)
(define (rollback) committed)
(define (commit) working)
(display (list 'working (map cdr working) 'rolled-back (map cdr (rollback)) 'committed (map cdr (commit))))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: Bare, it is a duplicate: equal? yes, eq? no, and there is nothing else to say. On a calibration bench it becomes an as-found record -- the technician adjusts the live offsets and the copy preserves what the instrument read before anyone touched it, so the drift is computable afterwards. Lifted to transactions it becomes isolation: the working copy absorbs every speculative write, and committing or rolling back is nothing more than choosing which of the two names to keep. Same call each time. What climbs is what the untouched original is FOR -- nothing, then evidence, then the ability to undo.
row-3-dimension.meta: The third rung is the reason the verb exists in a list library at all. Copy-on-write transactions are the general case, and 'save the old values' is the special case where the transaction is never rolled back.
row-3-dimension.eng: An as-found record is a copy taken before the work starts. Taking it after, or taking a shallow one, produces a document that agrees with itself and with nothing else.
row-3-dimension.math: Two objects with the same graph are interchangeable for every question about VALUES and distinguishable for every question about identity. Mutation is what makes the distinction observable.
row-3-dimension.cs: Copy-on-write is how versioned state is built without a log. The copy is the version, and the branch point is wherever the copy was taken.

row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (nothing-is-shared? al)
  (let ((c (alist-copy al)))
    (and (not (eq? c al))
         (let loop ((x c) (y al))
           (cond ((null? x) #t)
                 ((eq? (car x) (car y)) #f)
                 (else (loop (cdr x) (cdr y))))))))
(display (map nothing-is-shared?
              (list '((a . 1)) '((a . 1) (b . 2)) '((a . 1) (b . 2) (c . 3)) '((a . 1) (a . 1)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (writes-do-not-escape? al)
  (let* ((c (alist-copy al))
         (before (map cdr al)))
    (for-each (lambda (e) (set-cdr! e 'clobbered)) c)
    (and (equal? (map cdr al) before)
         (equal? (map cdr c) (map (lambda (_) 'clobbered) c)))))
(display (map (lambda (n) (writes-do-not-escape? (list-tabulate n (lambda (i) (cons i i)))))
              '(1 2 3 5)))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: The copy is equal? to the original for every alist including the empty one and ones with duplicate keys; no entry pair in the copy is eq? to the corresponding entry in the original; and set-cdr! on every entry of the copy leaves the original completely unchanged.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all alists a. equal?(alist-copy(a), a); and for all i. not eq?(nth(alist-copy(a), i), nth(a, i)); and mutating every cdr of the copy leaves every cdr of a at its former value
row-4-proof.meta: The third program is the one that matters, because it tests the PROPERTY rather than the representation: it does the mutation the verb exists to make safe and checks the original survived. The first two would still pass under an implementation that copied one level too shallow -- no, the second would not, which is why both are here. Duplicate-key alists are included because a copy that deduplicated would break equal? and would be a different verb.
row-4-proof.eng: Clobbering the copy and finding the original intact is the only test that actually exercises the guarantee. Comparing with equal? tests that it copied SOMETHING.
row-4-proof.math: Equality of value together with distinctness of identity, at every position, is precisely what 'a copy' means. Either half alone is a weaker and useless claim.
row-4-proof.cs: Testing an aliasing guarantee requires mutation. A purely functional test suite cannot distinguish a correct alist-copy from the identity function.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (checkpoint state) (alist-copy state))
(define (with-attempted-edits state edits)
  (let ((work (checkpoint state)))
    (for-each (lambda (e)
                (let ((hit (assq (car e) work)))
                  (if hit (set-cdr! hit (cdr e)))))
              edits)
    (if (>= (cdr (assq 'balance work)) 0) work state)))
(define account (list (cons 'balance 100) (cons 'fees 0)))
(define ok (with-attempted-edits account '((balance . 60) (fees . 40))))
(define refused (with-attempted-edits account '((balance . -5))))
(display (list 'accepted (map cdr ok) 'refused (map cdr refused) 'source (map cdr account)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (duplicate-map f) (alist-copy f))
(define (compose-maps f g)
  (map (lambda (p)
         (let ((hit (assv (cdr p) (duplicate-map g))))
           (cons (car p) (if hit (cdr hit) 'undefined))))
       (duplicate-map f)))
(define f '((1 . 10) (2 . 20) (3 . 30)))
(define g '((10 . a) (20 . b)))
(display (compose-maps f g))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (fork state) (alist-copy state))
(define (branch-and-measure state writes)
  (let ((child (fork state)))
    (for-each (lambda (w)
                (let ((hit (assq (car w) child)))
                  (if hit (set-cdr! hit (cdr w)))))
              writes)
    (length (filter (lambda (p) (not (equal? (cdr p) (cdr (assq (car p) state))))) child))))
(define base (list (cons 'a 1) (cons 'b 2) (cons 'c 3)))
(display (list 'one (branch-and-measure base '((a . 9)))
               'two (branch-and-measure base '((a . 9) (c . 9)))
               'none (branch-and-measure base '((a . 1)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: alist-copy makes an alist whose entries can be mutated without the original noticing.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: checkpoint is one call; with-attempted-edits builds a whole speculative transaction out of it -- apply every edit to the copy, check an invariant, and return the copy or the untouched original. Rejection costs nothing because the original was never touched. math: duplicate-map is one call; compose-maps uses it to build the composition of two finite maps by looking each image up in the second, producing a new map defined exactly where the chain is. cs: fork is one call; branch-and-measure diffs the branch against its parent, which is the primitive underneath every version-control and every change-detection scheme.
row-5-emergence.meta: All three build the same machine: fork, mutate freely, compare or choose. The copy is what makes 'mutate freely' safe, and once it is safe, the surrounding logic gets to be straight-line imperative code instead of a careful functional rebuild. The verb buys back mutation.
row-5-emergence.eng: Validate-then-commit is only cheap if abandoning the attempt is free. That is exactly what a copy purchases.
row-5-emergence.math: Composing finite maps is lookup chained through an intermediate; the result is defined on a subset of the first map's domain, and the undefined points have to be represented, not dropped.
row-5-emergence.cs: A diff against a parent is the whole of change detection. Fork, write, compare -- and every one of those three steps needs the fork to have been deep enough.
